lens: Predictive coding / DPCM expert (SZ3, Gorilla, LFZip lineage): treat TRACQ as a 2D-grid DPCM codec whose predictor, quantizer feedback loop, and residual entropy stage are all currently leaving 3-5 orders of magnitude of rate-distortion on the table.

proposals.name: P1: Closed-loop (quantization-in-the-loop) encoding
proposals.mechanism: Replace the open-loop vectorized percent grid (core_enhanced.py `_compute_raw_percent_grid`, which computes P[i,t] from ORIGINAL neighbors and lets the decoder cumprod quantized values) with classic DPCM closed-loop encoding: the encoder maintains the decoder's reconstruction x_hat. At each step t it computes p[t] = 100*(x[i,t] - x_hat[i,t-1]) / max(|x_hat[i,t-1]|, eps), clamps, mu-law-quantizes to the SAME code the decoder will see, dequantizes it, and updates x_hat[i,t] = x_hat[i,t-1]*(1 + p_hat/100). The decoder in `reconstruct_from_quantized` is ALREADY the matching closed-loop decoder (the cumprod path) — only the encoder changes. Anchors (`anchor_interval`) become unnecessary and are removed.
proposals.why_it_wins: This is the root cause of failure modes 1 and 2. Open-loop, per-step quantization errors enter a multiplicative recursion and compound without bound: the log-error random-walks with variance growing O(T), which is exactly the MetroPT-3 RMSE 3.8e95 blowup at T=1.5M. Closed-loop, each step's error is bounded by half a quantization cell in percent space regardless of T: |x[t]-x_hat[t]| <= |x_hat[t-1]|*(C_i/100)*(delta_q/2), where delta_q is the local mu-law cell width. For mu=255, 8-bit, the cell near zero (where almost all real percent changes live) is (2/256)*ln(1+mu)/mu ~ 1.7e-4 of the clamp; with C_i ~ 50% that is a per-step relative error of ~4e-5 of |x| — i.e. the standing error drops from unbounded/1e2-scale to ~1e-4*|x|, recovering roughly 3-6 orders of magnitude of RMSE at IDENTICAL bit rate (the code grid is the same size). This is the textbook DPCM fix (Jayant & Noll); SZ3 and LFZip are both closed-loop for exactly this reason.
proposals.expected_gain: MetroPT-3 unanchored: RMSE 3.8e95 -> O(0.01-1) (bounded, no drift) at the SAME 0.0297 ratio minus anchor overhead; the multi-MB JSON anchor payload disappears, so ratio also improves (anchors at interval 100 cost ~n_vars*8B/100 steps raw, several bytes/step as JSON text). UCI Air Quality 8-bit: RMSE 108.3 -> order 0.01-0.1 at the same ~0.114 ratio (per-step half-cell error ~1e-4..1e-3 of signal magnitude instead of compounding). Zero rate cost; pure distortion win.
proposals.implementation_sketch: In core_enhanced.py add `closed_loop: bool = True`. New encoder method `_encode_closed_loop(self, bits)` replacing the compute_percent_grid->quantize path: sequential loop over t with all variables vectorized per step (numpy: recon = data[:,0].copy(); for t in 1..T-1: p = 100*(data[:,t]-recon)/np.maximum(np.abs(recon),eps); clip to clamps; y = compander.compress(p/clamps); q[:,t-1] = round((y+1)/2*levels); p_hat = expand(deq)*clamps; recon *= 1+p_hat/100). Mirror core.py's HAS_NUMBA pattern with an njit kernel `_encode_closed_loop_numba(data, clamps, mu, levels, eps)` for the 1.5M-step MetroPT case. Clamps still computed from a first open-loop pass (`_compute_adaptive_clamps` unchanged). Delete anchor emission; keep decoder as-is. Metadata gains one flag `closed_loop: true`.
proposals.risk: Encode becomes sequential in t: pure-numpy loop over 1.5M steps is ~10-60 s (fine for benchmarks but the encode-MB/s table will show a drop vs the vectorized open-loop); numba kernel restores >100 MB/s. Second risk: if a clamped step cannot represent the needed change (true change > C_i), closed-loop keeps trying to catch up over subsequent steps — behavior is bounded but error can plateau at the clamp-limited rate; mitigated by the escape mechanism in P2. Near-zero reconstruction values still make percent space touchy (eps guard) until P2 moves to value-space residuals.
proposals.preserves_image_artifact: Fully. The output is still one mu-law code per variable per timestep, same (n_vars, T-1) uint8/uint16 grid, same PNG path in codec.py. Pixels are visually near-identical to the current image (they differ from open-loop codes only by the small quantization-feedback term), so visual inspection and compressed-domain anomaly detection are unaffected — and anchors no longer punch exact-value discontinuities into the reconstruction.
proposals.interactions: Prerequisite for everything else: P2's error bound is only valid closed-loop; P3/P4 predictors must predict from reconstructed (not original) values or they reintroduce drift. Synergy with the entropy stage: closed-loop residuals are slightly more concentrated than open-loop percent changes, marginally helping PNG/Zstd. Conflicts with nothing; `anchor_interval` becomes dead code.

proposals.name: P2: Error-bounded value-space residual quantizer with centered sparse code grid
proposals.mechanism: Change the quantization domain from 'mu-law of percent change' to SZ-style error-bounded residual coding, closed-loop: user specifies per-point bound e_i (absolute, or relative via e_i = e_rel * scale_i with scale_i a per-variable amplitude stored in metadata — this is the new 'adaptive quantization'). Encoder: r = x[i,t] - x_pred[i,t] (x_pred from P1/P3 predictor, in VALUE space, no division); integer code k = round(r/(2*e_i)); reconstruction x_hat = x_pred + 2*e_i*k, guaranteeing |x - x_hat| <= e_i at every point. Codes are stored as pixel = k + 128 (uint8, k clipped to [-127,127]) or k + 32768 (uint16); |k| overflow emits an escape code (pixel 0) plus the exact float32 stored in a side array. Entropy stage: the code grid goes to PNG as today for viewing, but the shipped bitstream is Zstd of the code bytes (container.py already has the Zstd path), because the grid is now overwhelmingly {127,128,129}-valued and Zstd/DEFLATE finally has skew to exploit.
proposals.why_it_wins: Fixes failure modes 3, 4, and 5 simultaneously. (a) Information-theoretically, the current mu-law output deliberately spreads codes over the full [0,255] range (that is what companding does), so DEFLATE sees ~8 bits/pixel of apparent entropy — which is why lossy TRACQ (0.05-0.22) barely beats lossless Delta+Zstd (0.12-0.24). A dead-zone uniform quantizer on prediction residuals concentrates mass at k=0: for Laplacian residuals with std sigma_r and bound e ~ sigma_r, code entropy is ~1-2.5 bits/sample; the entropy coder then delivers ratio ~ H/64 vs float64, i.e. 0.02-0.04 — 4-8x below lossless. (b) Value-space residuals eliminate the near-zero percent-change instability (no division anywhere), retiring the auto_offset heuristics. (c) The user gets a hard per-point max-error guarantee like SZ3/ZFP, which the paper reviewers explicitly demanded. This is exactly SZ3's quantizer architecture (linear-scale quantization + unpredictable-value escape), which is the proven rate-distortion frontier for time-series-like data.
proposals.expected_gain: UCI Air Quality: at e set to match ZFP tol=1e-1's RMSE 0.004 (e ~ 0.007, since RMSE ~ e/sqrt(3) for uniform error), expect 3-6 bits/sample -> ratio 0.05-0.10 vs ZFP's 0.273 at equal RMSE: a 3-5x Pareto win over ZFP. Against SZ3 expect parity within ~1.3-2x size (SZ3 has a stronger entropy coder). MetroPT-3: with e ~ 0.05*std per variable, RMSE ~0.03*std at ratio ~0.01-0.03 — beats the paper's anchored point (RMSE 1.71 @ 0.0297) on BOTH axes while keeping per-timestep resolution that PAA-1024 destroys. Lossy-vs-lossless gap (failure 3): ratios drop to 3-8x below Delta+Zstd.
proposals.implementation_sketch: In core_enhanced.py add mode `quantizer='error_bound'` with params `abs_error` and/or `rel_error` (per-variable e_i = max(abs_error, rel_error*np.std(data[i]) ) stored in metadata as 'error_bounds'). Inside the P1 closed-loop kernel replace the mu-law branch: k = np.rint((x[:,t]-pred)/(2*e)); esc = np.abs(k)>127; q[:,t-1] = np.where(esc, 0, k+128).astype(np.uint8); exact values data[esc,t] appended to an escape list (indices implicit from pixel==0); recon = np.where(esc, exact, pred+2*e*k). Escape list packed as float32 + Zstd, sizes counted honestly in the ratio. Add `to_zstd_bytes()` using the existing zstandard dependency for the shipped artifact; keep ImageCodec.save_png for the viewable artifact. Benchmark hooks: extend scripts/rate_distortion.py to sweep e over (1e-3..1e-1)*std to draw a real R-D curve against zfp_sweep/sz3_sweep in baselines.py.
proposals.risk: Escape-heavy channels (spiky, heavy-tailed) could bloat the side array — monitor escape fraction and fall back to 16-bit codes (k+32768) per variable when >1-2%. The mu-law/percent identity of TRACQ is diluted: adaptive quantization survives as per-variable e_i selection, but reviewers may ask what remains novel vs SZ3 — the honest answer is the image-grid artifact and compressed-domain visual analytics, so the paper must lean on that. Zstd-of-codes vs PNG DEFLATE must be reported as the primary size (PNG kept as the view artifact) or the PNG container overhead eats ~10-20% of the win on small datasets.
proposals.preserves_image_artifact: Yes, and arguably improves it: the grid is still exactly one pixel per variable per timestep; mid-gray (128) = 'perfectly predicted', brightness deviation = innovation magnitude. Anomalies now pop visually as bright/dark pixels on a flat gray field — strictly better for visual inspection than the current full-range mu-law texture. Escape pixels (value 0) mark 'unpredictable' events, which is itself an anomaly overlay.
proposals.interactions: Requires P1 (the bound only holds closed-loop). Supersedes mu-law for the R-D-optimal path (keep `use_mu_law` as a legacy/visualization mode; the two quantizers are alternatives, not composable). P3/P4 shrink sigma_r, which directly shrinks code entropy at fixed e — every bit of predictor improvement is a pure rate win here. The entropy stage change (Zstd on centered codes) only pays off because this proposal creates the skew.

proposals.name: P3: Per-variable predictor bank (previous / linear / seasonal-lag), closed-loop
proposals.mechanism: Replace the fixed order-1 'previous value' predictor with a small bank, chosen per variable and recorded as one byte each in metadata: (0) previous: x_pred = x_hat[t-1]; (1) linear extrapolation / 1D Lorenzo-2: x_pred = 2*x_hat[t-1] - x_hat[t-2] (this is delta-of-delta in Gorilla terms); (2) seasonal: x_pred = x_hat[t-L] + (x_hat[t-1] - x_hat[t-L-1]) with per-dataset lag L detected from the autocorrelation peak of the first differences (electricity: L=24 or 96/144 depending on sampling; traffic: daily/weekly lag). Selection: one open-loop pilot pass computes residuals under each predictor and picks argmin of estimated code length sum(log2(2*|r|/(2e)+1)) (a robust entropy proxy), per variable. All predictors read only reconstructed values, keeping P1's guarantee.
proposals.why_it_wins: The brief's root-cause list is explicit: 'Only an order-1 previous-value predictor is used.' For smooth sensor channels (temperature, pressure in MetroPT-3, gas concentrations in Air Quality), the signal is locally near-linear, so linear extrapolation shrinks residual variance by the classic factor: if first differences have lag-1 autocorrelation rho, second differencing reduces residual variance by ~2(1-rho) relative to first differencing — for rho=0.9 that is 5x variance (=2.3 bits/sample at fixed e). SZ3 ships Lorenzo + linear-regression predictors for exactly this reason and it is where most of its rate advantage over delta coding comes from. Conversely, for white-noise-dominated channels, linear extrapolation is WORSE (residual variance 3x higher: var(2nd diff of white noise)=6sigma^2 vs 2sigma^2), so per-variable selection is not optional — it is the mechanism that makes the bank safe. Periodic loads (electricity/traffic) are the extreme case: the seasonal predictor removes the dominant daily component that no order-2 temporal predictor can see, typically 3-10x residual std reduction on strongly periodic series.
proposals.expected_gain: At fixed error bound e (P2), rate falls by the entropy of what the better predictor removes: expect 1-2.5 bits/sample on smooth channels (Air Quality sensor channels, MetroPT analog pressures) -> a further 25-50% ratio reduction on top of P2 (e.g. 0.06 -> 0.035-0.045 at unchanged RMSE). On electricity/traffic-style periodic datasets, seasonal-lag prediction is worth 1.5-3.3 bits/sample (3-10x residual std), often the difference between losing and winning against SZ3 there. On noisy channels: zero loss by construction (selector falls back to predictor 0).
proposals.implementation_sketch: In core_enhanced.py: `_select_predictors(self, e)` — pilot pass in pure numpy on ORIGINAL data (selection quality barely differs from closed-loop): r0 = np.diff(x); r1 = np.diff(x, n=2); rS = (x[:,L+1:]-x[:,L:-1]) - (x[:,1:-L]-x[:,:-L-1]) ... compute per-variable code-length proxy for each, argmin -> pred_ids (np.uint8 array, stored in metadata as 'predictors'). Lag detection: `_detect_season_lag` via np.argmax of the mean ACF of first differences over lags [16, T//4] (FFT autocorrelation, ~5 lines). Extend the P1/P2 numba kernel with a branch on pred_id and a ring view of the last max(L,2)+1 reconstruction columns (keep a (n_vars, L+1) rolling buffer; for L up to a few hundred this is trivial memory). Warm-up steps (t<2 or t<L+1) use predictor 0. Metadata additions: 'predictors', 'season_lag'.
proposals.risk: Seasonal predictor needs the rolling reconstruction buffer in the sequential kernel — modest complexity, and a wrong detected lag L silently degrades to noise-level gains (guard: only enable predictor 2 if its pilot code length beats predictor 1 by >0.3 bits/sample). Regime changes mid-series make a single per-variable choice suboptimal (SZ3 switches per block); acceptable v1 simplification, or add per-block (e.g. 4096-step) predictor ids later for ~1 byte/block overhead. Selection on original rather than reconstructed data is slightly optimistic but second-order at reasonable e.
proposals.preserves_image_artifact: Yes — the artifact is still the (n_vars, T-1) residual-code grid from P2; only what the pixel is a residual AGAINST changes per row. Rows using different predictors remain directly comparable visually (all centered at gray = predicted). Optionally tint row labels by predictor id in the viewer; the PNG itself is unchanged in shape and semantics.
proposals.interactions: Multiplies with P2: predictor gains convert 1:1 into rate at fixed error bound. Requires P1's closed-loop discipline (predict from x_hat only). Mild overlap with P4: on datasets where channels are correlated because they share a periodic driver, P3's seasonal predictor and P4 capture some of the same redundancy — apply P3 first, then let P4's selector decide if cross-channel residual correlation remains.

proposals.name: P4: Cross-channel residual prediction (intra-timestep)
proposals.mechanism: After temporal prediction (P1/P3), exploit inter-sensor correlation WITHIN each timestep: order variables so correlated channels are adjacent (reuse the existing `_compute_variable_order` greedy correlation ordering, repurposed from a PNG-filter trick into a decode dependency order); for each non-root variable i, pick a reference channel ref(i) earlier in the order and a coefficient beta_i (least squares on pilot residuals), and encode d_i[t] = r_i[t] - beta_i * r_hat_ref(i)[t], where r_hat_ref is the reference's already-DEQUANTIZED residual at the same t (decoder-available, so the closed loop stays exact). Decoder processes variables in stored order within each timestep: r_hat_i = 2*e_i*k_i + beta_i*r_hat_ref(i). beta_i and the order go in metadata; channels whose residual correlation is below threshold get beta=0 (independent).
proposals.why_it_wins: The brief lists 'no cross-channel exploitation' as a verified root cause, and the target datasets are the best case for it: UCI Air Quality has paired channels (PT08.Sx sensor responses vs reference concentrations of the same gases) with inter-channel correlation of changes rho ~ 0.6-0.9; MetroPT-3 pneumatic pressures/currents co-move. Linear prediction from one reference reduces residual variance by (1-rho^2): rho=0.8 -> 2.8x variance (0.74 bits/sample); rho=0.9 -> 5.3x (1.2 bits/sample). No competitor in the benchmark exploits this (ZFP's 2D transform partially does, which is a reason it is not embarrassed on multivariate grids; SZ3 in the repo runs per-dataset but its Lorenzo is spatial-agnostic across unrelated rows) — so this is TRACQ's chance at a structural advantage native to its 2D-grid framing: the grid's vertical axis becomes an exploited dimension, not just a storage layout.
proposals.expected_gain: 0.5-1.2 bits/sample on the correlated subset of channels; dataset-level, expect a further 10-30% ratio reduction on Air Quality (many correlated pairs) and 5-20% on MetroPT-3, at unchanged RMSE/error bound. Smallest expected payoff of the four proposals, but it is the only one that gives TRACQ an axis the baselines cannot match, which matters for the paper's narrative as well as the numbers.
proposals.implementation_sketch: Pilot pass (numpy): residual matrix R (n_vars, T-1) under the chosen P3 predictors on original data; corr = np.corrcoef(R); order via existing `_compute_variable_order`; for each i in order[1:], ref(i) = argmax over already-placed j of |corr[i,j]|, beta_i = corr[i,ref]*std_i/std_ref if |corr|>0.3 else 0. In the sequential kernel, within each t iterate variables in `order` (or vectorize as a sparse triangular update: r_hat = solve of (I - B) structure — with a tree dependency it is one gather + multiply per variable, still vectorizable as beta[order]*r_hat[ref_idx] computed in dependency order; a single loop over a topological levels list keeps it numpy-fast). Metadata: 'var_order', 'ref_idx', 'betas'. Escape-coded (unpredictable) reference values participate via their exact reconstruction, so the chain never breaks.
proposals.risk: Gains evaporate if temporal predictors already explain the shared structure (correlation of RESIDUALS, not signals, is what pays — measure it in the pilot and auto-disable). Error-bound bookkeeping: with d_i quantized to +/-e_i, the reconstruction error of r_i stays <= e_i because beta*r_hat_ref is decoder-exact — the guarantee survives, but this must be asserted in tests. Adds the most code complexity per bit gained; ship last, keep behind a flag. Static beta over the whole series underfits regime changes (same per-block remedy as P3 if needed).
proposals.preserves_image_artifact: Yes — pixels are still per-variable-per-timestep residual codes on the same grid; rows are now 'conditioned on' a sibling row, which visually FLATTENS correlated rows to gray except where a channel deviates from its usual coupling — i.e. the image highlights cross-sensor anomalies (one sensor breaking correlation), a genuinely new visual-analytics capability to feature in the paper.
proposals.interactions: Builds on P1+P2, ordered after P3 (predict residuals of the residuals). Repurposes `reorder_variables` machinery — the correlation ordering now has a functional decode role, so the old PNG-filter rationale and this cannot use different orders (use this one; PNG filtering benefit is retained anyway since correlated-conditioned rows compress similarly). More zero codes -> stronger entropy-stage payoff. Slight tension with per-variable e_i: reference channels should get the tighter bound since their error feeds dependents (bounded, not compounding, but worth a note).

overall_assessment: P1 (closed-loop encoding) matters most: it is the root cause of the 3-5 order-of-magnitude RMSE gap and the MetroPT-3 divergence, costs zero rate, deletes the anchor machinery (including its multi-MB JSON tEXt overhead), and the existing cumprod decoder already implements its decode side — only the encoder loop changes. But P1 alone does not fix the weak ratios (failure mode 3) because mu-law codes still fill the full byte range. The combination I would ship is P1+P2 as a single unit — closed-loop, value-space residuals, user-specified per-variable error bound, centered sparse code grid, Zstd bitstream with PNG retained as the viewable artifact — which is architecturally SZ3-with-an-image-artifact and should beat ZFP outright on the UCI datasets (expect ~3-5x smaller at equal RMSE) and dominate the paper's own anchored MetroPT-3 point on both axes. Then add P3 (per-variable predictor bank with seasonal lag) for a further 25-50% rate cut and competitiveness with SZ3 on smooth/periodic data; P4 (cross-channel residual prediction) last, behind a flag, as the paper's differentiator: 10-30% extra on correlated datasets plus a novel cross-sensor visual-anomaly capability no baseline offers. Benchmark honestly by extending scripts/rate_distortion.py to sweep the error bound and plotting full R-D curves against zfp_sweep/sz3_sweep, Delta+Zstd, Gorilla, and PAA from tracq/baselines.py, counting escape-list and metadata bytes in every ratio.
